subject.title: Fragment 1: Sea-ward, white gleaming thro' the busy scud
subject.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
subject.text:
Sea-ward, white gleaming thro' the busy scud
With arching Wings, the sea-mew o'er my head
Posts on, as bent on speed, now passaging
Edges the stiffer Breeze, now, yielding, drifts,
Now floats upon the air, and sends from far
A wildly-wailing Note.

title: The Gull Coleridge Watched at Least Three Times
standfirst: This six-line notebook sketch of a gliding sea-mew carries no date anywhere in Coleridge's papers, and nobody printed it until 1912. It was not the only time he wrote this bird down, and it was not the only time he cut it back out again.

sections.heading: Three Nows and No Argument
sections.body:
The gull in this fragment changes its mind four times and the poem stops there. It "posts on, as bent on speed," then "edges the stiffer Breeze," then, "yielding, drifts," then "floats upon the air" — four different relations to the wind, tracked across six lines by someone who was plainly standing still and watching the whole time. The syntax does the tracking: "now passaging," "now, yielding, drifts," "Now floats" — three nows in a row, each one correcting the last, with no fourth clause to resolve them into a single motion. It ends on the bird's cry rather than on anything the watcher makes of it: "sends from far / A wildly-wailing Note."

That restraint is the strange thing, set against how Coleridge normally used a bird. The albatross in *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* is a plot; the nightingale in his conversation poems argues with received opinion about what its song means. This gull argues nothing. There is no "I" in the six lines beyond the gull passing "o'er my head," and no turn where the bird's flight becomes a figure for the poet's own state, the move that finishes off so much of his other nature writing. It just glides, adjusts, glides again, and calls out. A sketch this pure of argument had nowhere obvious to go inside a Coleridge poem — which may be exactly why it never went anywhere.

sections.heading: The Same Bird, Written Down Twice
sections.body:
Coleridge did not watch a gull like this only once. Among a separate cluster the poet's grandson later labelled ["Fragments from a Notebook"](https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.29276), dated only "circa 1796-98" because it cannot be pinned down any closer, sits a five-word scrap numbered 29 in that sequence:

> The swallows
> Interweaving there, mid the pair'd sea-mews
> At distance wildly-wailing!

Swallows crossing paths with paired sea-mews, calling from a distance — and the same closing phrase, "wildly-wailing," that ends the six-line fragment above. The editorial note attached to our poem makes the link explicit rather than leaving it to a reader's ear: "Now first published from an MS. Compare Fragment No. 29 of Fragments from a Notebook." Two separate scraps of paper, two different bundles of manuscript, the same bird doing roughly the same thing, described with the same unusual compound. One made it into print in 1893. The other did not surface for another nineteen years, and unlike its sibling it carries no date at all — not even a guessed one.

sections.heading: A Speech Cut From the Stage
sections.body:
The image had already done real work once, in a script Coleridge wrote for the theatre rather than a notebook nobody but him would read. In [*Osorio*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osorio_%28play%29), his tragedy of 1797, the Moorish woman Alhadra stands alone on a moonlit mountainside, cut off from everyone she trusts, and wishes herself out of her own species entirely:

> O! would to Alla,
> The raven, or the sea-mew, were appointed
> To bring me food! or rather that my soul
> Could drink in life from the universal air!
> It were a lot divine in some small skiff
> Along some Ocean's boundless solitude,
> To float for ever with a careless course,
> And think myself the only being alive.

Here the sea-mew is not observed but envied: a scavenger fed by nobody, owing nothing to anybody, floating on a "careless course" through a solitude Alhadra finds preferable to human company. *Osorio* was turned down by Drury Lane and shelved for fifteen years. When Coleridge finally reworked it as *Remorse* for the same theatre in 1812, trimming the play down for a paying West End audience, this speech went with the cuts, alongside other passages judged too radical or too digressive for the stage version — a fate the same summary of the revision confirms in general terms, and one a search of *Remorse*'s printed text bears out line by line: the raven and the sea-mew do not appear in it at all. The public, finished version of the play lost the image. Coleridge's own notebooks kept it in circulation regardless.

sections.heading: The Editor Who Never Saw This One
sections.body:
The first person to go looking through Coleridge's manuscripts for material like this was [James Dykes Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dykes_Campbell), a Scottish businessman turned Coleridge scholar who had no formal training in the job and did it anyway. Campbell had left school at fourteen for a merchant's office in Port Glasgow, and only later, well into adulthood, turned to editing; his one-volume *Poetical Works*, with a biographical introduction, appeared from Macmillan in 1893, expanded the following year into a full biography. That 1893 edition was the first place many of Coleridge's stray notebook fragments reached print at all — Fragment 29, the swallows and the paired sea-mews, among them.

Campbell did not find everything. He died of heart failure in 1895, two years after his edition appeared, and the fragment about the lone gull "passaging" the breeze was not among his discoveries. Whatever manuscript page it was written on stayed unprinted, uncollected, and — as far as the record shows — unread by anyone preparing an edition for another nineteen years.

sections.heading: Found by the Poet's Grandson
sections.body:
It was [Ernest Hartley Coleridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Hartley_Coleridge), the poet's own grandson, who eventually printed it. Trained at Balliol and by then in his mid-sixties, he had already worked through the family's unpublished notebooks once before, drawing on them for *Anima Poetae* in 1895, and he returned to them for his *Complete Poetical Works* of 1912 — the edition still used as the standard reference today. His own headnote to the section explains the method plainly: fragments "published from MS. sources in 1893, or are now published for the first time," collected from Coleridge's notebooks and, where necessary, corrected against manuscripts Campbell had worked from only in copies. Ours falls in the second group. Its entire documented history reads: "Now first published from an MS." He would go on editing Byron and his own great-grandfather John Coleridge after this, and when he died in 1920 he was, by one account, the last of the family still working through its papers.

In his numbered list this six-line sketch sits as Fragment 2, directly after a stanza he dates to about 1787 and directly before one he can date to 1799 precisely. It alone carries no date at all — not "circa," not a guess, nothing. The nearest anyone has come to placing it in time is where Ernest Hartley Coleridge happened to file it: between a boy's schoolroom elegy and a cottage rhyme from 1799, in the company of two other scraps that share its habit of noticing a bird and then declining to make anything more of it.
